item.title: Diverging paths to dark-matter discovery
item.description: arXiv:2610.14137v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The scientific discovery of dark matter has been pursued in two very different methodological and epistemic contexts. A microphysical context centered around the laboratory detection of a new particle, and a macrophysical context based on the astronomical identification of a non-luminous gravitating component. The justification for the salience of methodological diversity is that these different methods are complementary ways to discovering aspects of the same entity. The weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) made this expectation scientifically credible by connecting a particle candidate to a cosmological abundance, experimental searches, and explanations of astronomical phenomena. What happens to this connection when the WIMP loses its central position? I analyze 201,627 NASA Astrophysics Data System records to examine the organization of research following the decline of WIMP prominence. Astrophysics and high-energy physics remain jointly dominant, while WIMP-related mentions decline in both fields and successor candidates receive different degrees of attention. Concept networks show that WIMP-related research remains central across the literature, even as cross-field connections become less concentrated around it. These indicators measure research attention; they do not establish what scientists would accept as a discovery. I interpret the findings through a framework distinguishing constitutive identification, cosmic attribution, explanatory adequacy, and the cross-domain identification needed to connect them. A particle, compact-object population, or gravitational theory can resolve different parts of the inherited problem, and a partial or multicomponent discovery can leave other parts open. 'Diverging paths' describes this branching of possible resolutions.
item.dc:creator: Simon Allz\'en

item.title: Joint Trust-Distrust Structure Shapes Belief Propagation and Collective Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.14565v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Belief propagation in social networks depends on how trust and distrust jointly shape interpersonal influence. We develop a network model that treats trust and distrust as distinct but statistically coupled quantities. Their joint values determine the net trust and uncertainty of each relationship, and a neighbor can influence an agent only when both threshold conditions are satisfied. We show that the correlation between trust and distrust reshapes the transition between consensus and fragmentation by changing the availability of influential neighbors. Network connectivity also affects this transition, whereas degree heterogeneity has a more limited effect when networks have comparable mean degree. Moreover, the availability of influential neighbors alone does not determine the final consensus: correlations between relational properties and network degree can select agents with different degree compositions, altering the direction and magnitude of collective belief. Finally, we introduce a comfort index that quantifies the expected availability of influential neighbors and analytically links the joint trust-distrust structure to collective dynamics. Our results establish a mechanistic connection between relational structure, effective social influence, and emergent collective belief states.
item.dc:creator: Mozhgan Khanjanianpak, Yu-Ru Lin

item.title: Multi-Agent Learning of Reactive Strategies in Iterated Games
item.description: arXiv:2610.15054v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learning agents, whether humans or algorithms, adapt to one another rather than to a fixed environment. Selfish learning need not produce a good outcome for the group, especially when learners face a social dilemma. The iterated prisoner's dilemma (IPD) is the classical example, but it is usually studied in populations of agents who imitate successful strategies. Here, we instead study selfish gradient ascent learners on the two-dimensional space of reactive strategies. A reactive strategy is described by two continuous traits: reciprocity, the chance of cooperating after the co-player cooperates, and forgiveness, the chance of cooperating after the co-player defects. Each learner updates its strategy in the direction that most rapidly improves its payoff against all other learners, by an amount governed by its learning rate. We show that heterogeneity in learning rates can qualitatively change the long-term outcome: a population with uniform learning rates converges to always-defect (ALLD), whereas a population with variable learning rates approaches generous-tit-for-tat (GTFT), which produces nearly optimal collective payoffs. In simulations, every population passes through a transient state of minimal forgiveness, in which the distribution of reciprocity determines the outcome. Variable learning rates promote cooperation because slow learners preserve high reciprocity until the population reaches this state. We prove sufficient conditions on the distribution of reciprocity for convergence to ALLD or to tit-for-tat (TFT). Variable learning rates also allow cooperation to recover from perturbation, which is provably impossible under uniform learning. These results suggest that purely selfish and myopic learning can produce persistent cooperation provided the population has intrinsic variability in learning rates.
item.dc:creator: James P. Wolfe, Joshua B. Plotkin

item.title: Financial Interactions and Collective States: Part III. Description of Dynamic Collective States
item.description: arXiv:2610.15719v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a series of papers, we analyzed the mechanisms of capital allocation and accumulation among firms, investors, and banks within the framework of Field Economics. At the macro level, we found that multiple collective states may emerge, each organized in groups of agents characterized by distinct levels of disposable capital, returns, and stakes across sectors. This multiplicity of collective states reflects the inherent instability and default-prone nature of financial markets. It also underscores the necessity of transitions among these states. These transitions were not fully accounted for in our previous description of collective states, where we only considered marginal fluctuations around equilibrium levels. To fill this gap, the present paper aims to characterize the possible dynamic mechanisms underlying transitions between these collective states. It reviews and extends our previous analysis by examining their probability and stability. By introducing the notion of dynamic sub-collective states, it explores potential patterns of transition-such as morphing, merging, or splitting-among collective states. This study thus provides the foundational tools and analytical framework that will be employed to develop a field-theoretic description of dynamic collective states.
item.dc:creator: Pierre Gosselin (IF), A\"ileen Lotz

item.title: A Shy Voter Model: Entropy Flux in Opinion Formation
item.description: arXiv:2610.16053v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Some voters conceal their opinions, causing a mismatch between visible and private opinions in polls. Conventional voter models do not account for such concealment. Here, we introduce a shy voter model that incorporates a hidden state in addition to two visible states, as an extension of the conventional majority-rule voter model. The model exhibits continuous and hybrid transitions, yielding a rich phase diagram organized by the hidden fraction, i.e., the fraction of voters in the hidden state. For a large hidden fraction, the system undergoes a hybrid transition from the ordered state to the symmetric (disordered) state, whereas for a small hidden fraction, it exhibits a continuous transition, with a tricritical point separating the two regimes. Near criticality, both the order-parameter variance and the susceptibility diverge. The hidden fraction also governs the entropy flux, a quantity that is not directly observable in real-world situations. Thus, opinion concealment qualitatively reshapes opinion dynamics, while the present framework provides a basis for further extensions toward more realistic forms of social interactions.
item.dc:creator: Cook Hyun Kim, Sangjoon Park, B. Kahng

item.title: Towards modelling abreast to in-file transitions in small pedestrian groups
item.description: arXiv:2610.16400v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pedestrians in a crowd largely walk in small groups, dyads above all, and modelling how these groups arrange themselves is a step towards realistic models of the crowd as a whole. A dyad walks side by side in a dilute crowd and one behind the other in a dense one, an abreast to in-file transition recently measured in real life across the full range of naturally occurring crowd conditions (van der Laan and Corbetta, PLOS ONE 2026). The cost-function models of dyad formation by Zanlungo and coworkers (Phys. Rev. E 2014; EPL 2015) hold the pair abreast and have no in-file minimum at any finite density. Building on them, we propose and analyse a qualitative model in which the transition appears as an effective density parameter grows: the two formations become minima that coexist over a window of densities and exchange stability within it. We quantify this transition by computing the Orientation Log-Odds $\Pi_\text{OLO}$ as predicted by the model. This paper is a first step towards quantitative models of dyads and of their formation transitions.
item.dc:creator: Alessandro Corbetta, Chiel van der Laan, Francesco Zanlungo

item.title: Foundations for a Lens of Quantum Governance
item.description: arXiv:2610.16939v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The second quantum revolution is a revolution of information. Advances in quantum computation, communication, and sensing offer new capabilities while raising questions about how quantum infrastructures will be organised, accessed, and governed. We argue that their significance for governance lies not in transforming political principles, but in how their technical and infrastructural requirements may affect existing relationships of authority, responsibility, legitimacy, and power. This paper develops a quantum governance lens that connects governance scholarship with quantum information science, examining interactions between technical design, institutional arrangements, and infrastructural dependencies. We apply this lens to five areas: quantum computation, quantum key distribution, Quantum Byzantine Agreement, blind quantum computation, and dual-use quantum sensing. These applications illustrate how technical capabilities may influence access, trust, privacy, oversight, and accountability, while demonstrating that technical guarantees cannot resolve institutional questions independently. We conclude that quantum technologies do not necessarily introduce unique governance challenges or require entirely new governance frameworks. Rather, they provide a context in which established questions of legitimacy, accountability, and equity must be reconsidered in relation to emerging technological capabilities and institutional choices.
item.dc:creator: Shira K. Huizing Lemstra, Tzula B. Propp

item.title: Behavioural Sociology of Humans and Machines
item.description: arXiv:2610.17487v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly participates in communication, decision-making, and collective action, making the social organisation of human-machine interaction central to Hybrid Intelligence (HI). This chapter reviews the behavioural sociology of humans and machines through an HI lens, examining how interaction and feedback shape the combination of human and artificial capabilities. Drawing on sociology, social psychology, human-computer interaction, organisational studies, collective intelligence, and science and technology studies, it traces processes from individual social perception to cooperation in hybrid groups and organisational and institutional arrangements. Particular attention is given to how machine participation alters familiar mechanisms: social categorisation attaches expectations to designed identities, reciprocity may involve unequal social obligations, and algorithmic recommendations acquire authority through organisational practices. The chapter distinguishes observable machine behaviour from human interpretations of intention, understanding, and moral responsibility. It also considers how behavioural effects can extend beyond direct human-machine encounters, while separating established findings from proposed longer-term consequences. It argues that the benefits of HI depend on how roles, incentives, reliance, and accountability are organised, and identifies priorities for empirical research on these evolving sociotechnical arrangements.
item.dc:creator: Taha Yasseri, Hao Cui, Nico Mutzner

item.title: Collective Benefits and Efficiency in Coupled Echo State Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.17506v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simple aggregation of independent responses ("wisdom of crowds") generally improves collective performance through statistical facilitation, but interaction among members can sometimes hinder group outcomes. However, under certain circumstances, coordination studies show that interacting groups can outperform their individual members and nominal groups, and interaction can also be more efficient than independence. We present a reservoir computing model to investigate how interaction can enhance joint performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Echo state networks were trained independently to identify Japanese speakers from vowel recordings and tested jointly with and without coupled feedback. Model pairs reproduced the dyadic advantage reported by Bahrami et al. (2010) with interaction via pooled-feedback, but not when independent responses were aggregated together. Model dynamics revealed that interaction was beneficial whereas aggregated outputs were prone to diverging from runaway feedback over time. In terms of efficiency, larger groups of smaller interacting models outperformed smaller groups of larger models while equating for total amount of group computation. Our results offer a formal framework for explaining when and why interaction enhances collective intelligence.
item.dc:creator: Polyphony Bruna, Rick Dale, Michael J. Spivey, Christopher T. Kello

item.title: Hurricane recovery gaps lie in reconnection, not local restart
item.description: arXiv:2610.17550v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Climate-intensified hurricanes disrupt urban mobility, yet whether recovery is equitable across the rural-urban gradient is unclear. Analyzing device-based mobility for Hurricanes Helene and Milton, we find local activity restarted within approximately 4.5 days in both storms, whereas reconnection to the outside world took 5 days in coastal-urban Florida but 11 in inland-rural Appalachia. The gap lies in external reconnection, not local restart, implying planners should target rural isolation.
item.dc:creator: Angelina Liu, Mengqiu Cao, Sen Pei, Qing Yao

item.title: Replacement distance controls growth at long wavelengths in a coevolving spatial network
item.description: arXiv:2610.17764v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When an agent leaves a spatial network, its replacement removes old contacts and may transport population to a new location. The frequency of replacement alone therefore does not determine how turnover changes spatial organization. We study diffusing agents joined by persistent attractive contacts, with the total pull on each agent bounded. At fixed population, successors appear at the departure position, within a surrounding disk, or anywhere in the system. We ask whether small differences between dense and dilute regions grow or fade. The theory separates an exactly calculable diffusion and replacement contribution from an approximate attraction contribution obtained by averaging the contact network. Paired simulations find similar attraction contributions under the three rules at all nine sampled wavelengths. Changing only the replacement location reverses the broadest tested pattern: it grows with replacement at the departure position but fades under both displaced rules. An independent radius scan traces this change from growth to decay. Under displaced replacement, intermediate wavelengths grow between sampled long and short scales with decay. Rates measured in the earliest finite window are compatible with the prediction at long and intermediate wavelengths; discrepancies are already present at short wavelengths. Replacement distance thus helps determine which spatial density contrasts are initially amplified.
item.dc:creator: Ruiwu Niu, Ming Yuan, Ying-kit Wong

item.title: Social Norm Diffusion in Societies: Simple or Complex?
item.description: arXiv:2610.18501v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Social norms are a fundamental component of society, shaping how we communicate, cooperate, and avoid conflict. Despite their ubiquitous presence and profound influence on behaviour, questions remain about how they spread from person to person and whether they are adopted. Using an evolutionary game-theoretic model, we study whether simple or complex contagion processes characterise how social norms spread. Crucially, contagion type is endogenous and emerges from the model. We also vary cultural conformism, the cost of following a norm, and network topology to assess the generality of our results. We show that social norms in our model can spread through simple contagion when a new norm is low in cost and cultural conformism is low, while norms spread through complex contagion when the new norm is costly and cultural conformism is high.
item.dc:creator: Claudia Lorenzetti, Aron Szekely, Daniele Vilone, Giulia Andrighetto

item.title: Directed percolation in higher-order social dilemmas
item.description: arXiv:2610.18506v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multiplayer social dilemmas on hypergraphs show a variety of emergent phenomena, which has been attributed to group interactions. Here we test whether pairwise dynamics can reproduce them as well. We derive the mesoscopic Langevin equation of a testbed model and find the operator content of absorbing phase transitions: a directed-percolation line, a tricritical point, and a first-order region whose spinodal is the explosive transition. In our analysis, three-player games only set the values of the Landau coefficients. We construct a strictly pairwise model with short-lived memory, in which every event involves at most two entities, that reproduces these coefficients term by term and has exactly the same mean-field fixed points. Simulations confirm that the two dynamics share mean-field critical and tricritical scaling and the size of the critical mass, and that a purely three-player game on a two-dimensional triangular lattice lies in the directed-percolation class. For these games, the explosive transition and the critical mass therefore do not require group interactions, and the critical behavior is that of the pairwise theory.
item.dc:creator: Pablo Villegas, Sandro Meloni

item.title: Multilateral governance of invasive alien species management: An ecological-economic model with Allee effect
item.description: arXiv:2610.14916v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Invasive alien species (IAS) generate substantial ecological and economic damages that often transcend political boundaries, creating strong incentives for coordinated management. We develop a two-region ecological-economic model of IAS control that integrates prevention and eradication measures with population dynamics characterized by logistic growth and an Allee effect. We derive analytical results on the interaction between ecological thresholds and strategic behaviour and compare outcomes under cooperation (central planner) and non-cooperation (open loop Nash equilibrium and Markovian Nash equilibrium). We show that, under realistic control costs, neither prevention nor eradication can eliminate invasive populations in finite time, and complete prevention of cross-border spread is generally not optimal. In the absence of an Allee effect, the zero-population equilibrium is unstable, implying long-run persistence of the invasive species. By contrast, the presence of an Allee effect fundamentally alters system dynamics by making extinction locally stable and creating a basin of attraction within which eradication becomes feasible. This finding highlights the economic significance of ecological thresholds and demonstrates how delays in management can shift populations beyond critical levels, after which eradication is unlikely regardless of subsequent control efforts. Numerical simulations further show that cooperative management expands the set of initial conditions leading to eradication and consistently reduces aggregate social costs relative to decentralized management. The results provide a formal rationale for rapid intervention, precautionary regulation, and stronger multilateral cooperation in IAS management, particularly in jurisdictions such as the European Union where listing and control actions may be delayed pending evidence of harm.
item.dc:creator: Raouf Boucekkine, Weihua Ruan, Ullrika Sahlin

item.title: An Approximate-Master-Equation Formulation of the Watts Threshold Model on Hypergraphs
item.description: arXiv:2503.04020v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In traditional models of behavioral and opinion dynamics on networks, researchers suppose that interactions occur between pairs of individuals. However, in reality, social interactions also occur in sets of three or more individuals. A common way to incorporate such polyadic interactions is to study dynamical processes on hypergraphs, in which interactions can occur between any number of the individuals. A major current effort is to generalize popular dynamical processes from graphs to hypergraphs. One important model is the Watts threshold model (WTM), which describes a simplistic social spreading process and was extended recently by Chen et al. from dyadic networks (i.e., ordinary graphs) to polyadic networks (i.e., hypergraphs). In the present paper, we extend their discrete-time model to continuous time by using approximate master equations (AMEs). By employing AMEs, we are able to very accurately model the mean behavior of the continuous-time system. We reduce the high-dimensional AME system to a system of three coupled ordinary differential equations without any detectable loss of accuracy. This much lower-dimensional system is computationally faster to solve numerically, and it is also easier to interpret. We linearize the reduced AME system and derive a cascade condition, which allows us to determine when a large spreading event occurs. We then examine our reduced AME system on a contact hypergraph of a French primary school and on a hypergraph of computer-science coauthorships. We find that our full and reduced AME systems give reasonably good descriptions of the mean time-dependent fraction of active nodes in the polyadic WTM dynamics on these empirical networks.
item.dc:creator: Leah A. Keating, Kwang-Il Goh, Mason A. Porter

item.title: Temporal patterns of preferences through Wikipedia editing in different languages
item.description: arXiv:2603.01299v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Temporal editing patterns on Wikipedia provide a computational lens on cultural dynamics across linguistic communities. We analyse a decade of editorial activity (2001--2010) in eleven Wikipedia language editions and apply hierarchical clustering to two representations of collective behaviour: a static one, based on the thematic composition of each edition, and a temporal one, based on its weekly activity cycle within each thematic category. For the temporal representation we compare two normalisations: one retains only the shape of the weekly cycle, and the other combines it with thematic composition. The linguistic communities exhibit distinct circadian and weekly editing rhythms. Some groupings are recovered by both representations and by both activity metrics (edits and editors), most notably Russian and Chinese, whereas others, such as German and French, emerge only from temporal activity rhythms. Temporal information thus reveals structure that thematic composition alone does not, which points to time as a relevant and often neglected dimension in cross-cultural analyses of digital trace data, and in studies that use online platforms as proxies for collective cultural behaviour.
item.dc:creator: David Andr\'e Villamil Carrillo, Y\'erali Gandica

item.title: LLM-DR: An On-Demand Delivery Simulation Framework for Studying Heterogeneous Rider Behavior and Collective Mobility with Persona-Grounded Large Language Model Agents
item.description: arXiv:2603.12559v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: On-demand delivery platforms are computational social systems in which dispatch rules and repeated rider actions jointly shape service and urban mobility. Riders choose whether to reject offers, accept one order, or bundle several orders; assignments then change their availability and other riders' opportunities. Modeling this feedback requires empirical rider heterogeneity, shared-order interaction, and road-network execution to be represented together. Delivery optimization and large language model (LLM) mobility generation provide useful foundations, but leave this combination insufficiently examined. We develop Large Language Models as Delivery Riders (LLM-DR), an agentic simulation framework for benchmarking rider policies under a common order stream and dispatch protocol. Persona-grounded LLM agents provide a reference implementation, using empirical profiles, local observations, short-term memory, and route-tool estimates to propose order actions. The environment resolves assignment conflicts, constructs pickup and drop-off sequences, and executes tool-supported routes. Analysis of 9,025 Beijing orders and a sample of 2,508 routed delivery waves identifies four rider personas. A controlled single-day reconstruction places 60 agents, equally distributed across personas, in an observed stream of 8,656 orders. Persona groups complete 16-30 orders per rider, with average bundle sizes of 1.116-2.212. Distributional comparisons retain several empirical persona orderings in order volume, bundling, and routed-wave distance. Fleet-level outcomes show displaced demand, service-occupancy, and completion peaks, alongside a shared central service core and differentiated spatial reach. These results connect data-derived rider strategies to executable action chains and collective mobility patterns within a shared computational social system.
item.dc:creator: Chengbo Zhang, Zekai Jin, Kaihan Zhang, Zihan Yang, Qinyu Cui, Zuopeng Xiao, Jiangbo Yu

item.title: Local network evolution rules driving shortest path multiplicity
item.description: arXiv:2605.25237v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The shortest path multiplicity, here denoted by $\mu$, is an important metric of complex networks. For real networks $\mu$ is high and it correlates with the network community structure. Since local network evolution induces network communities, it is possible that a high shortest path multiplicity is the natural expectation of local evolution rules. Here I demonstrate, by means of numerical simulations and exact results, that this is indeed the case. For random graphs with arbitrary degree distributions $p_k$, $\langle\mu\rangle\sim \langle k(k-1)\rangle / (\langle k\rangle e)$, growing with the network size when $p_k\sim k^{-\gamma}$ and $\gamma\leq3$. For networks generated by stochastic local rules, $\langle\mu\rangle$ increases with the network size and it does so faster than what is observed in their randomized versions. Furthermore, the number of communities increases with the network size and the correlation with $\langle \mu\rangle$ follows.
item.dc:creator: Alexei Vazquez

item.title: From risk to flourishing: Seeds for responding to a complex world
item.description: arXiv:2607.19685v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Complex risk arises when interacting hazards, infrastructures, ecological systems, institutions, and human behaviors produce nonlinear impacts that cannot be inferred from any component in isolation. We call the study of these dynamics complex risk science. Flourishing is the actualization of all beings toward their good--individually and collectively--answering the question of `how do we live well with and for each other?'. In science as in society, the tendency to reduce, segregate, specialize, and settle has precluded embracing the concept of flourishing as a guiding principle. We describe how complex risk science reframes risk science research so that it can promote the flourishing of socio-ecological-technological systems, and explore how its practice may point society toward a more flourishing future. Our exploration mirrors the unsettled and searching nature of flourishing: examine ideologies traditionally believed to be rigidly in opposition and consider what emerges in the space(s) and conversation between them. We call this a dialectical approach: not a means of resolving contradiction, but a practice of sustaining it, so that systems, and our understanding of them, remain capable of reframing as conditions change. Within this dialectical paradigm, we revisit longstanding tensions in risk science: physical|social, determinism|uncertainty, and contextuality|generality. Examining the conversation among these tensions reveals five seeds that are dispositions for practicing complex risk science: interdependence, responsivity, participation, pluralism, and ongoingness. They can support any scientific endeavor to embrace complexity and promote flourishing. Practicing these seeds at scale will depend on institutional reform: creating collectives toward complex risk science, supporting them with skillfully governed commons, and centering care in our research and evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Ryan M. McGranaghan, Elisabeth H. Krueger, Alexandre Dunant, Guillaume Falmagne, Lynee L. Turek-Hankins, Sara M. Constantino, Raissa D'Souza, Elke U. Weber, Graydon W. Manzke

item.title: Breathing chimera states from purely triadic interactions
item.description: arXiv:2607.28017v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Chimera states, characterized by the coexistence of synchronized and desynchronized dynamics in identical oscillators, are typically studied in systems with pairwise interactions. Recent studies have shown that purely higher-order interactions can support chimera states. Here, we show that breathing chimera states arise in a model governed solely by a triadic phase interaction, whose intrinsic $\pi$-symmetry permits bimodal phase distributions. We construct a bimodal Ott-Antonsen reduction that incorporates an asymmetry parameter via prescribed asymmetric initial conditions, thereby achieving an exact low-dimensional description of the macroscopic dynamics. This allows us to derive an analytic condition for the emergence of chimera states and identify a bifurcation to a breathing chimera regime characterized by persistent oscillations. Furthermore, the reduced dynamics can be expressed as a Riccati-type equation, providing a geometric interpretation of the chimera state as a closed periodic orbit in the complex plane. Our results establish purely triadic coupling as a minimal higher-order mechanism for chimera formation and provide a tractable framework for studying symmetry-broken collective dynamics in systems dominated by many-body interactions.
item.dc:creator: Sudo Yi, Gug Young Kim, Mi Jin Lee, S. -W. Son, B. Kahng

item.title: The hierarchical organization of urban social overlap: How shared social spaces diverge from physical mobility
item.description: arXiv:2609.12888v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Cities are commonly characterized through population density, infrastructure, and mobility flows. These quantities describe where people are and how they move, but movement does not uniquely determine where populations repeatedly encounter one another or whether different locations participate in the same social environments. Here, we construct co-presence overlap networks across 13 Brazilian cities to distinguish these dimensions of urban organization. We introduce two complementary measures: colocation, which quantifies recurrent co-presence activity within individual locations, and co-connectedness, which measures the extent to which locations share the same co-present pairs. We find that the spatial concentration of colocation differs substantially from that of mobility, producing social centers that can differ in both number and location from mobility centers. At the network level, co-connectedness exhibits a non-random hierarchical organization in which locations preferentially share recurrent pairs with locations of similar activity. This hierarchy is systematically weaker and substantially more variable across cities than the corresponding mobility hierarchy, demonstrating that cities with similar mobility organization can differ in how recurrent social overlap is organized across locations. Finally, we show that the spatial proximity of colocation activity to social centers relative to residential centers provides a complementary spatial dimension of urban organization. Together, these results separate three features that are conflated when cities are characterized through mobility alone: movement between locations, local opportunities for social interaction, and the organization of recurrent social overlap across locations.
item.dc:creator: Bibandhan Poudyal, Mariana Macedo, Ronaldo Menezes, Gourab Ghoshal

item.title: Community-Centers Identify Robust Biomarkers in High-Dimensional, Low-Sample-Size Gene Expression Data
item.description: arXiv:2610.00986v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: High-dimensional, low-sample-size bulk gene expression data poses a fundamental challenge in transcriptomics, which typically includes tens of thousands of genes but relatively few samples, leading to overfitting and unstable selection for key features as biomarkers. We propose a regression by community centers (RCC) framework tailored for such data. RCC converts gene expression data into a feature proximity network and leverages the phase transition of the giant connected component to identify a critical distance threshold that yields a sparse yet maximally informative network representation, indicated by a minimum normalized shortest compression length. Intuitively, at the criticality, the network balances fragmentation and over-connectivity, allowing meaningful gene-gene associations communities to emerge while filtering noises, such that community-centers capture the most informative and non-redundant signals. These representative genes are then fed to a simple ordinary least squares (OLS) model for downstream predictions. Across five bulk gene expression datasets, RCC displays exceptional prediction performance, clearly outperforming benchmark methods, remains robust to missing data and noises, and does not rely on external biological knowledge. These results suggest that network-based representations provide an effective and general framework for high-dimensional, low-sample-size prediction tasks beyond transcriptomics and illustrate how network-science ideas can support robust learning in data-scarce regimes.
item.dc:creator: Ruiqi Li, Te Bai, Renaud Lambiotte, Orr Levy, Paul Expert, Daqing Li, Shlomo Havlin

item.title: The benefit of ignorance for traffic through a random congestible network
item.description: arXiv:2503.09684v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When traffic is routed through a network that is susceptible to congestion, the self-interested decisions made by individual users do not, in general, produce the optimal flow. This discrepancy is quantified by the so-called ``price of anarchy.'' Here we consider whether the traffic produced by self-interested users is made better or worse when users have uncertain knowledge about the cost functions of the links in the network, and we define a parallel concept that we call the ``price of ignorance.'' We introduce a simple model in which fast, congestible links and slow, incongestible links are mixed randomly in a large network and users plan their routes with finite uncertainty about which of the two cost functions describes each link. One of our key findings is that a small level of user ignorance universally improves traffic, regardless of the network composition. Further, there is an optimal level of ignorance which, in our model, causes the self-interested user behavior to coincide with the optimum. Many features of our model can be understood analytically, including the optimal level of user ignorance and the existence of critical scaling near the percolation threshold for fast links, where the potential benefit of user ignorance is greatest. We demonstrate that our qualitative conclusions apply also to networks with nonlinear cost functions, and we comment on the case of scale-free networks, where there is no direct analog of percolation physics.
item.dc:creator: Alican Saray, Calvin Pozderac, Ari Josephson, Shravan Sripadhanallur Natarajan, Brian Skinner

item.title: Network Reconstruction in Consensus Algorithms with Hidden Agents
item.description: arXiv:2604.05709v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reconstructing the parameters that encode the influence between model variables based on time-series measurements represents an outstanding question in the theory of complex network-coupled systems. Here, we propose a solution to this problem for a class of noisy leader-follower consensus algorithms, where one has access to measurements only from the followers but not from the leaders. Leveraging the directed Laplacian coupling of such systems, we present an autoregressive expansion of the observed dynamics which can be truncated at different orders, depending on the memory of the leaders. When their memory is short, this allows one to correctly reconstruct the full dynamical matrix with hidden leader agents, provided some additional assumption on the system to lift the degeneracy in the reconstruction. We illustrate and check the theory using numerical simulations for the cases of both a single and multiple hidden leaders.
item.dc:creator: Melvyn Tyloo

item.title: Characterizing Opinion Evolution of Networked LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2606.18276v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly interact with one another in multi-agent systems, from simulations of human discourse to influence operations and fully LLM-driven social platforms. These interactions give rise to new regimes of opinion propagation that are not yet well understood. We investigate whether classical opinion dynamics models, which have long been used to explain how interactions shape collective beliefs in human societies, can capture the behavior of LLM networks. Specifically, we quantify the relative contributions of classical opinion-dynamics mechanisms, including neighbor influence, stubbornness, homophily, and bias, to the evolution of LLM opinions. Among the mechanisms considered, a bias term capturing regression toward a model- and topic-dependent opinion emerges as a significant explanatory component, with its inclusion reducing cumulative estimated mean opinion error by up to $88\%$. We additionally observe similar trends across the evaluated model families, discussion topics, and network structures.
item.dc:creator: Caleb Probine, Yigit Ege Bayiz, Filippos Fotiadis, Samuel Li, Yunhao Yang, Ufuk Topcu

item.title: Six objects reported at 480 mph in a declassified military infrared video show brightness flicker at bird wingbeat rates
item.description: arXiv:2610.08692v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In September 2026 the U.S. Department of War released an infrared video recorded from a military aircraft over the Middle East, with a mission report describing six small spherical objects moving at an estimated 480 miles per hour. We measure the brightness of each object in every frame. All six brighten and dim steadily at 7.1-7.9 times per second, each at its own rate and out of step with the others. Tests with planted constant-brightness objects show that neither compression nor the sensor produces this flicker. The same analysis, applied to the Galileo Project's ground-based infrared cameras near Las Vegas, finds flying animals beating steadily at 3.4-10.0 times per second, within the range of bird wingbeats. A nearly stationary object at 60-80% of the aircraft's height would produce the reported ground-projected speed of 480 miles per hour. The six objects are best explained as a small flock of birds flying nearer to the aircraft than the crew assumed. The same analysis also finds seven objects with similar beats, at 3.0-11.0 times per second, in four other released military videos. More broadly, this work shows that even heavily redacted videos of unidentified anomalous phenomena can be analyzed using reproducible, quantitative methods to test specific hypotheses. Releasing the redacted sensor and platform data would provide information that could refute these hypotheses.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Haqq-Misra, Ravi Kopparapu, Richard Cloete, Omer Eldadi, Michael Shermer, Abraham Loeb
